after:
The crowd’s posture changed before the Dohkar could speak. A woman in the front rank—her skin the color of wet slate, her Weave-Script flaring in sharp, accusing lines—stepped forward with her hand already lifted as if to ward off contamination.

“You broke the seal,” she said. The words carried across the crimson spiralgrass without effort. “You reached for her rite the moment the wish turned.”

Murmurs rose behind her like a tide. Another voice, lower, from a man whose long black hair was bound back with a single silver cord: “She was the one the girl named. The father crossed the Ascendant Run three turnings ago and asked after her at the landing. Now the answer stands in front of us.”

I felt the weight of every alignment-sense in the clearing press against me at once. My own Weave-Script answered without permission, flickering across my forearms in defensive, broken spirals that only made the accusation look truer. The youth knelt where she had been placed, coral hair trembling against her cheek, her small aqua hands clenched in the grass. She had meant the wish as kindness. The Dohkar’s eyes stayed on me, waiting for the explanation that would only make the picture worse.

I tried to speak. The words came out muffled and wrong behind the torn gossamer still hanging from my face. I pulled the last of it free with fingers that shook once, then steadied.

“The wish was never hers to offer,” I said. “She changed the desire mid-rite. The sacrifice no longer matched the request. I moved because the misalignment was already forming. I did not reach for the wish. I tried to stop it from twisting.”

A low sound moved through the assembled First Favored, not quite agreement and not quite dismissal. Someone at the edge muttered about protocol. Another answered that protocol had already been broken when the girl’s words left the path they had rehearsed. The woman with the slate skin exhaled through her teeth.

“You were sealed,” she said. “Sealed supervisors do not speak into another’s rite. You tore the band yourself. The girl’s sacrifice now carries your name in it. The Dohkar will have to answer for that before the Chayr.”

The youth looked up at me then, eyes wide and wet. She had offered her discipline because she wanted to train as a Sacrificiant. She had offered it to me. The price she named could not cover the new desire, and now the cost was being taken from my account instead. I could feel the Dohkar’s alignment-sense reading every line of my Weave-Script, every flicker of guilt and fear that I could not hide. There was no clean way to say that the girl had tried to give me something I had never asked for and that I had moved only because the rite itself was already breaking.

Julian’s memory returned without invitation—the way he had lifted the child at the festival, the long black hair swinging forward, the calm in his voice when he told the merchant to leave. He would have known how to stand in a moment like this without making it worse. I wanted that stillness now, and the wanting only sharpened the distance between us. He was not here. The clearing waited for me to finish the sentence I had begun, and every word I could find sounded like an excuse.

The Dohkar’s hands remained lifted, the warning still in place. The crowd’s posture had not softened. I stood with the torn gossamer in one hand and the deck in the other, the weight of both suddenly heavier than they had any right to be.

I realize that old tarot deck is still in my hand. Reassuringly solid. Present. One of the heavy gold cards slips out — "Petition Fate" is inscribed on it.
